records.quote: Counterexample 2.1. Consider the Weibull family F̄θ (t) = e−θt^α , t ≥ 0, α > 1, θ > 0. Since Hθ (t) = θtα , we have Lθ (t) = tHθ′ (t)/Hθ (t) = α, t > 0, so the F RAI function is independent of θ. ... for θ1 ≠ θ2 , [µθ1/µθ2 limits unequal] hence µθ1 and µθ2 are not proportional. Therefore, by Theorem 2.2, Lµθ1 ≢ Lµθ2 . Thus, equality of the F RAI functions does not imply equality of the corresponding M RLAI functions.
records.compared: FRAI equality vs MRLAI equality across proportional hazards

conclusion.direction: Lθ1 = Lθ2 (FRAI equal) but Lµθ1 ≢ Lµθ2 — FRAI equality ↛ MRLAI equality

records.quote: Counterexample 3.1. Let X1 and X2 be two random variables with respective M RL functions µX1 (t) = 1/(1 + t), and µX2 (t) = 1/{2(1 + 2t)}, so that the corresponding M RLAI functions ... are decreasing in t > 0. ... X having survival function F̄X (t) = 0.2 F̄X1 (t) + 0.8 F̄X2 (t) ... the corresponding M RLAI function ... is non-monotonic as Figure 12 shows. Hence, the class of DM RLAI distributions is not closed under mixtures.

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI NOT closed under mixtures

records.quote: Counterexample 3.2. Let Xi , i = 1, 2, be two i.i.d. non-negative random variables with M RL function µXi (t) = (1 + t)−1/10 , t ≥ 0. ... each Xi belongs to the DM RLAI class. Now, write X = max{X1 , X2 }. ... Numerical integration gives LµX (0.1) ≈ 0.9701, LµX (2) ≈ 0.8528, and LµX (20) ≈ 0.8981, showing that LµX (t) is non-monotone. Hence, the DM RLAI class is not closed under the formation of a parallel system [and hence k-out-of-n / coherent systems].
records.compared: DMRLAI closure under parallel systems (max of 2)

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI NOT closed under parallel systems (hence not under k-out-of-n or coherent systems)

records.quote: Counterexample 3.3. Let X1 and X2 be i.i.d. lifetime random variables with common M RL function [piecewise: 2 (0≤t≤5/2); 2−(3/125)(t−5/2) (5/2<t≤5); (97/125)(15/2−t) (5<t<15/2)]. ... each component belongs to the DM RLAI class. Now, let X1:2 = min{X1 , X2 } ... Figure 13(b) shows that LµX1:2 (τX x) is non-monotone. Hence, the DM RLAI class is not closed under the formation of a series system.
records.compared: DMRLAI closure under series systems (min of 2)

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI NOT closed under series systems

records.quote: Counterexample 3.4. Let X1 and X2 be i.i.d. standard exponential random variables, which may be considered as DM RLAI. Then ... LµXi = 1 ... take Xc = X1 + X2 . The survival function of Xc is F̄Xc (t) = (t + 1)e−t , whereas ... µXc (t) = (t + 2)/(t + 1). Then ... LµXc (t) = t(t + 2)/[(t + 1)(ln(t + 1) + t)] which is non-monotone as LµXc (0.20) = 0.9590531, LµXc (3.0) = 0.8549358, and LµXc (10.0) = 0.8799147. Thus ... DM RLAI class is not closed under convolution.

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI NOT closed under convolution (also used for IMRLAI, since exponential is both)

records.quote: Counterexample 3.5. Let X1 and X2 be two random variables with respective M RL functions µX1 (t) = 1 + 8t and µX2 (t) = 1 + 0.1t ... which are both increasing [IMRLAI]. Consider now X with survival function F̄X (t) = 0.2(8t + 1)−9/8 + 0.8(0.1t + 1)−11 ... Figure 14 shows that LµX (t) is non-monotonic. Consequently, the IM RLAI class is not closed under mixture.

conclusion.direction: IMRLAI NOT closed under mixtures

records.quote: Counterexample 3.6. Let X1 and X2 be two i.i.d. random variables with survival function F̄X1 (t) = (1 + t)−2 ... µXi (t) = 1 + t, giving LµXi (t) = 2(1 + t)/(2 + t), which is increasing ... Now, write X = max{X1 , X2 }. ... [numerics] which is non-monotone, as is clear from Figure 15. Hence, the IM RLAI class is not closed under the formation of a parallel system [hence not k-out-of-n or coherent systems].

conclusion.direction: IMRLAI NOT closed under parallel systems (hence not k-out-of-n / coherent systems)

records.quote: Counterexample 3.7. Let X1 and X2 be i.i.d. lifetime random variables with common M RL function µX (t) = 1 + 5√t, t ≥ 0. Then LµX (t) = (1 + 5√t)/(1 + (10/3)√t) which is increasing in t. Thus each component belongs to the IM RLAI class. ... X1:2 = min{X1 , X2 } ... Numerical integration gives LµX1:2 (1) ≈ 1.5577, LµX1:2 (4) ≈ 1.5778, and LµX1:2 (25) ≈ 1.5649. Thus LµX1:2 (t) is not nondecreasing. Hence, the IM RLAI class is not closed under the formation of a series system.

conclusion.direction: IMRLAI NOT closed under series systems

a_records.quote: Counterexample 4.4. Let X and Y have Erlang densities fX (t) = 9te−3t and fY (t) = 4te−2t , t ≥ 0. Then F̄X (t) = (1 + 3t)e−3t and F̄Y (t) = (1 + 2t)e−2t . A direct calculation gives [double-integral ratio] = 3e^t (2t + 3)/[4(t + 1)] whose logarithmic derivative is 1 − 1/[(2t + 3)(t + 1)] > 0. Hence X ≤vrl Y . On the other hand, ... R(t) := [∫0^t µX ]/[∫0^t µY ] = 4{3t + ln(3t + 1)}/[9{2t + ln(2t + 1)}] ... R(0.1) = 0.653742 > R(1.5) = 0.628701 < R(5) = 0.637118, R(t) is not nonincreasing. Therefore X ≰MRLAI Y , showing that X ≤vrl Y does not imply X ≤M RLAI Y .

conclusion.direction: X <=vrl Y but X ≰MRLAI Y — the two orders are incomparable

b_records.quote: Counterexample 4.4. Let X and Y have Erlang densities fX(t) = 9te^{−3t} and fY(t) = 4te^{−2t}, t ≥ 0, respectively. ... Hence X ≤vrl Y. On the other hand ... R(t) = 4{3t + ln(3t + 1)}/{9{2t + ln(2t + 1)}}. Since R(0.1) = 0.653742 > R(1.5) = 0.628701 < R(5) = 0.637118, R(t) is not nonincreasing. Therefore X ≰MRLAI Y, showing that X ≤vrl Y ⇏ X ≤MRLAI Y.
b_records.compared: vrl order holds but MRLAI fails

conclusion.direction: X <=vrl Y but X not <=MRLAI Y

a_dirs: componentwise mrlai does not imply mrlai of the maxima — lµx

a_records.quote: Counterexample 4.7. Let X1 and X2 be two i.i.d. random variables having Erlang distribution with survival function F̄Xi (t) = (1 + t)e−t , t ≥ 0. Also, let Y1 and Y2 be two i.i.d. random variables having exponential distribution with survival function F̄Yi (t) = e−2t , t ≥ 0. ... LµXi (t) = t(t + 2)/[(t + 1)(ln(t + 1) + t)] < 1, whereas ... LµYi (t) = 1. Thus, Xi ≤M RLAI Yj , for all i, j = 1, 2. If we write X = max{X1 , X2 } and Y = max{Y1 , Y2 }, ... from Figure 17, the curves of LµX (t) and LµY (t) intersect. Therefore, the M RLAI order is not preserved under the formation of a parallel system [hence not coherent systems].

conclusion.direction: componentwise MRLAI does NOT imply MRLAI of the maxima — LµX and LµY curves intersect

b_records.quote: Counterexample 4.7. Let X1 and X2 be two i.i.d. random variables having Erlang distribution with survival function F̄Xi(t) = (1 + t)e^{−t}, t ≥ 0. Also, let Y1 and Y2 be two i.i.d. random variables having exponential distribution with survival function F̄Yi(t) = e^{−2t}, t ≥ 0. ... Thus Xi ≤MRLAI Yj for all i, j = 1, 2. If we write X = max{X1, X2} and Y = max{Y1, Y2} ... the curves of LµX(t) and LµY(t) intersect. Therefore, the MRLAI order is not preserved under the formation of a parallel system.
b_records.family: Xi iid Erlang-2(rate 1); Yi iid Exp(rate 2)
b_records.compared: componentwise MRLAI order fails to propagate to maxima

conclusion.direction: Xi <=MRLAI Yj for all i,j but LµX and LµY of the maxima cross — X not <=MRLAI Y

records.quote: Example 2.1. Let X have the Pareto type II survival function F̄X (t) = (1 + t/β)−α , t ≥ 0, α > 1, β > 0. ... assumptions of Theorem 2.7 are satisfied with ρ = 1. Moreover, LµX (t) = 2(β + t)/(2β + t) → 2 = 1 + ρ as t → ∞.

conclusion.direction: LµX(t) = 2(β+t)/(2β+t) → 2; µX regularly varying index ρ = 1

records.quote: Example 2.10. Consider a lifetime random variable X with M RL function µX (t) = 1 + t (0≤t≤1), (5 − t)/2 (1<t≤2), 3/2 (t>2). ... Since LµX (0.5) = 1.2, LµX (1) = 1.3333, LµX (2) = 0.9231, and LµX (3) = 0.9474, the M RLAI function is non-monotone. Further, ... the F RAI function is also non-monotone.

conclusion.direction: both LX and LµX non-monotone

records.quote: Example 2.11. Suppose a lifetime random variable X has survival function F̄X (t) = exp{−t − t2 /2}, t ≥ 0. Then rX (t) = 1 + t, and the corresponding F RAI function is LX (t) = 2(1 + t)/(2 + t), t > 0, which is strictly increasing; hence X is IAI. Further, ... µX (t) < 1/(1+t), ... µ′X (t) < 0, the M RL function is strictly decreasing. Hence, X is DM RL.

conclusion.direction: X is IAI and DMRL — increasing FRAI may accompany decreasing MRL

records.quote: Example 2.12. Consider a lifetime random variable X with survival function F̄X (t) = exp{−t1/2 e^{t/10} }, t ≥ 0. ... the F RAI function as LX (t) = 0.5 + t/10, which is strictly increasing in t. So, the distribution belongs to the IAI class. The M RL function ... is non-monotone as Figure 7 shows.

conclusion.direction: X is IAI but MRL non-monotone — IAI ↛ DMRL

records.quote: Example 2.13. Let a lifetime random variable X have survival function F̄X (t) = exp{−(2t − t2 )/4} (0 ≤ t < 1), 0 (t ≥ 1). ... LX (t) = 2(1 − t)/(2 − t). So, X belongs to the DAI class. ... µX (t) ... is strictly decreasing as Figure 8 shows.

conclusion.direction: X is DAI and DMRL

records.quote: Example 2.14. Let a lifetime random variable X have the survival function F̄X (t) = 1/(1 + t3/2 ), t ≥ 0. ... LX (t) = (3/2)t^{3/2}/[(1 + t^{3/2}) ln(1 + t^{3/2})] which is strictly decreasing in t. So, the distribution belongs to the DAI class. The M RL function ... first decreases and then increases, which is non-monotone, although X is DAI.

conclusion.direction: X is DAI but MRL non-monotone — DAI ↛ DMRL

records.quote: Example 2.15. Consider a random variable X with survival function F̄X (t) = (1 + t)−(1+t) , t ≥ 0, so that the corresponding hazard rate is rX (t) = 1 + ln(1 + t) ... LX (t) = t(1 + ln(1 + t))/[(1 + t) ln(1 + t)] ... the F RAI function LX (t) is non-monotone, attaining a maximum near t ≈ 5, while the M RL function µX (t) is strictly decreasing.
records.compared: non-monotone FRAI with strictly decreasing MRL (DMRL)

conclusion.direction: FRAI non-monotone while DMRL — non-monotone FRAI does not preclude DMRL

records.quote: Example 2.16. Consider a lifetime random variable X with hazard rate rX (t) = 1/(t + 1)2 + t/10 + 1/10, t ≥ 0, having the F RAI function as LX (t) = [2(t + 1)3 + 10]/[(t + 1)(t2 + 3t + 22)] which is non-monotone ... The corresponding M RL function ... is non-monotone.

conclusion.direction: both LX and µX non-monotone

records.quote: Example 2.2. Consider a random variable having the M RL function µX (t) = 1 + t/2 (0 ≤ t ≤ 1), t + 1/2 (t > 1). Then LµX (t) = (4+2t)/(4+t) (0<t≤1), 4t²+2t over 2t²+2t+1 (t>1) which is increasing in t > 0. ... LX (0.99) ≈ 0.8234, LX (1.01) ≈ 1.0879, LX (2) ≈ 0.7149, the F RAI function is non-monotone.

conclusion.direction: X is IMRLAI (LµX increasing) but FRAI non-monotone — IMRLAI ↛ IAI

records.quote: Example 2.3. Consider a random variable X having µX (t) = (1 + t)−1 , t ≥ 0 so that LµX (t) = t/[(1 + t) ln(1 + t)] which is decreasing in t > 0. However, for this distribution rX (t) = t(t + 2)/(t + 1) so that LX (t) = [t²(t+2)/(t+1)²]/[2 + t − ln(t+1)] which is non-monotone as Figure 2 shows.

conclusion.direction: X is DMRLAI but FRAI non-monotone — DMRLAI ↛ DAI

records.quote: Example 2.4. Let X have survival function F̄X (t) = exp{−t1/4 (1 + t)1/2 }, t ≥ 0. Then ... LX (t) = 1/4 + t/[2(1 + t)], which is increasing in t. Hence, X belongs to the IAI class. Further, ... LµX (t) ... shows that it is increasing. Therefore, X is also IM RLAI.

conclusion.direction: X is IAI and IMRLAI

records.ambiguity: MRLAI monotonicity shown graphically (Figure 3) via transform x = t/(1+t).

records.quote: Example 2.5. Consider a random variable X ∼ U (0, 1). Then ... LX (t) = t/[(1 − t)(− log(1 − t))] which is increasing in t. Since ... µX (t) = (1 − t)/2, ... LµX (t) = 2(1 − t)/(2 − t) which is decreasing in t.
records.compared: IAI but DMRLAI — FRAI increases while MRLAI decreases

conclusion.direction: X is IAI and DMRLAI

records.quote: Example 2.6. Let X have survival function F̄X (t) = exp{−(2t − t2 )/4} (0 ≤ t < 1), 0 (t ≥ 1). ... LX (t) = 2(1 − t)/(2 − t) is decreasing ... LµX (t) is decreasing on (0, 1), as illustrated in Figure 4.

conclusion.direction: X is DAI and DMRLAI

records.quote: Example 2.7. Let X have hazard rate rX (t) = 2/(1 + t), t ≥ 0. Then ... LX (t) = t/[(1 + t) log(1 + t)] which is decreasing in t > 0. Also, F̄X (t) = (1 + t)−2 , so that µX (t) = 1 + t ... LµX (t) = 2(t + 1)/(t + 2) which is increasing in t. Thus, X is DAI and IM RLAI.

conclusion.direction: X is DAI and IMRLAI

records.quote: Example 2.8. To see that a distribution may be IAI while having a non-monotone M RLAI, consider X with survival function F̄X (t) = (t + 3√t + 2)e^{−t−2√t}/2. ... It can be seen from Figure 5 that F RAI is increasing, whereas M RLAI is non-monotone.

conclusion.direction: X is IAI but MRLAI non-monotone — IAI ↛ IMRLAI

records.ambiguity: Same construction also yields IMRL (non-IMRLAI) in Remark 2.3(b): L(0.01)≈1.015, L(5.5)≈1.082, L(15)≈1.076.

records.quote: Example 2.9. Consider a random variable having an Erlang distribution with density fX (t) = 4te−2t , t ≥ 0. Then LX (t) = 4t²/[(2t+1)(2t − ln(2t+1))] which is decreasing ... the M RL function is µX (t) = (t + 1)/(2t + 1), so that LµX (t) = 4t(t + 1)/[(2t + 1)(ln(2t + 1) + 2t)] which is non-monotone as Figure 6 shows.

conclusion.direction: X is DAI but MRLAI non-monotone — DAI ↛ DMRLAI

records.quote: Theorem 2.10. Let X have finite positive mean and a positive continuous M RL function on [0, τX ). If X is DM RLAI (resp. IM RLAI), then LµX (t) ≤ (resp. ≥) 1 for all 0 < t < τX . ... Combining Theorems 2.8 and 2.10, we obtain DM RLAI ⊊ DM RLA and IM RLAI ⊊ IM RLA.
records.compared: class inclusions DMRLAI ⊊ DMRLA, IMRLAI ⊊ IMRLA

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI ⇒ LµX ≤ 1 ⇒ DMRLA; strict inclusions DMRLAI ⊊ DMRLA and IMRLAI ⊊ IMRLA

records.quote: Theorem 2.11. Assume that µX is differentiable and positive on the support (0, τX ). Then X is DM RLAI (resp. IM RLAI) if and only if LµX (t) ≥ (resp. ≤) 1 + tµ′X (t)/µX (t), 0 < t < τX .
records.compared: characterization of DMRLAI/IMRLAI via pointwise inequality

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI ⇔ LµX ≥ 1 + tµ′X/µX; IMRLAI ⇔ ≤

records.ambiguity: Remark 2.3: with Thm 2.10 gives DMRLAI ⊊ DMRL (Erlang f(t) = t²e^{−t}/2 counterexample: L(2.5)≈0.7767, L(5)≈0.7525, L(10)≈0.7721 non-monotone) and IMRLAI ⊊ IMRL.

records.quote: Theorem 2.12. Let {Xθ : θ > 0} be a proportional hazards family with survival functions F̄θ (t) = {F̄0 (t)}θ , 0 ≤ t < τ0 , and let H0 (t) = − log F̄0 (t). If H0 is positive and differentiable on (0, τ0 ), then Lθ (t) = L0 (t), 0 < t < τ0 . Hence, the F RAI function is invariant under the proportional hazards family.
records.compared: FRAI invariance across the PH family

conclusion.direction: Lθ(t) = L0(t) for all θ — FRAI constant across proportional hazards

records.ambiguity: MRLAI is NOT invariant in the PH family — see Counterexample 2.1.

records.quote: Theorem 2.2. The equality LµX (t) = LµY (t) holds for all 0 < t < τXY if and only if µX (t) = c µY (t) for all 0 < t < τXY , for some constant c > 0.
records.family: lifetime distributions with positive continuous MRL
records.compared: equality of MRLAI functions of two rvs

hypotheses.text: positive continuous MRLs on common support

conclusion.direction: LµX ≡ LµY iff µX = cµY (proportional MRL) — MRLAI equality up to MRL scaling

records.ambiguity: Basis for preorder/antisymmetry discussion of ≤MRLAI in Section 4 (p40).

records.quote: Theorem 2.4. Let X be a continuous lifetime random variable having M RLAI function LµX . If LµX (t) is independent of t for all t over the support X, then the support cannot be finite. Further, if LµX (t) = c for all t ∈ (0, ∞), then the distribution of X is exponential and conversely.

conclusion.direction: LµX ≡ c forces c = 1 and exponential; exponential ⇒ LµX ≡ 1

records.ambiguity: Contrast: constant FRAI characterizes Weibull (Nanda et al.), while constant MRLAI characterizes exponential.

records.quote: Theorem 2.5. Let X be a random variable defined on [0, τX ]. If µX is nonincreasing on [0, τX ), then LµX (t) ≤ 1 for all 0 < t < τX . The converse is not necessarily true. [counterexample: µX = 1−0.4t on [0,2), 0.1t on [2,3), 0.3 on [3,∞), giving non-monotone LµX < 1]

conclusion.direction: X DMRL ⇒ LµX(t) ≤ 1; converse false (piecewise-linear µX counterexample, Fig 1a)

records.ambiguity: Embedded counterexample shows DMRLA \ DMRLAI exists.

records.quote: Theorem 2.6. Let X be a random variable defined on [0, τX ]. If µX is nondecreasing on [0, τX ), then LµX (t) ≥ 1 for all 0 < t < τX . The converse need not hold. [counterexample: µX = 1+t on [0,5), 11−t on [5,6), 5 on [6,∞), non-monotone LµX > 1]

conclusion.direction: X IMRL ⇒ LµX(t) ≥ 1; converse false (Fig 1b)

records.quote: Theorem 2.8. Let X have a positive continuous M RL function on the support [0, τX ). Then X ∈ DM RLA if and only if LµX (t) ≤ 1 for all 0 < t < τX , and X ∈ IM RLA if and only if LµX (t) ≥ 1 for all 0 < t < τX .
records.compared: characterization of DMRLA/IMRLA classes via MRLAI ≤/≥ 1

conclusion.direction: DMRLA ⇔ LµX ≤ 1; IMRLA ⇔ LµX ≥ 1

records.quote: Theorem 2.9. Let X have a positive continuous M RL function µX on the support [0, τX ). Then X is DM RLAI if and only if AX is geometrically concave. Similarly, X is IM RLAI if and only if AX is geometrically convex.
records.compared: structural characterization of DMRLAI/IMRLAI via geometric concavity of A_X(t) = ∫0^t µX

conclusion.direction: DMRLAI ⇔ AX geometrically concave (log A_X(e^y) concave); IMRLAI ⇔ convex

records.quote: Theorem 3.1. Let n ≥ 1, and let X1 , . . . , Xn be i.i.d. absolutely continuous lifetime random variables over the support with common differentiable survival function F̄X , and M RL function µX (t) = a + bt, 0 ≤ t < τX , where a > 0 and b > −1. If X1:n = min{X1 , . . . , Xn }, then LµX1:n (t) = LµX (t), 0 < t < τX .
records.family: linear-MRL family µX = a + bt, a > 0, b > −1
records.compared: MRLAI invariance under series-system formation within linear-MRL family

hypotheses.text: Xi iid, µX = a + bt, a > 0, b > −1

conclusion.direction: LµX1:n ≡ LµX — series system preserves MRLAI function exactly; DMRLAI/IMRLAI preserved within linear-MRL family

records.ambiguity: Only within the linear-MRL family — not a general closure (cf. Counterexample 3.3).
